5711BDC0DFE701318D2E68A86D17958E.description: Create and apply a framework of aesthetic criteria for evaluating his or her own dance work and that of others.

57116F90DFE701318D2D68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast several subtly differing dance compositions in terms of space (for example, shape, pathways), time (for example, rhythm, tempo), and/or force/energy/movement qualities (for example, weight, flow).

57111C90DFE701318D2C68A86D17958E.description: Create a short dance and revise it over time, articulating the reasons for his or her artistic choices and describing ways that the dance was impacted by those choices.

5710C190DFE701318D2B68A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate and apply critical, creative, and analytic thinking in response to dance.

57101630DFE701318D2968A86D17958E.description: Create a dance and describe lighting, costumes, props, and other scenic elements that would contribute to its meaning.

570FBA00DFE701318D2868A86D17958E.description: Create a dance sequence and select accompaniment (for example, sound, music, spoken text) that supports its meaning.

570F66C0DFE701318D2768A86D17958E.description: Analyze the main idea, theme, or feeling of a dance in relation to a personal context.

570F14B0DFE701318D2668A86D17958E.description: Create and perform brief dance compositions that communicate personal ideas, experiences, feelings, concepts, or images.

570EC550DFE701318D2568A86D17958E.description: The student will use dance as a medium to communicate meaning and/or artistic intent.

570E1800DFE701318D2368A86D17958E.description: Translate basic motif description/dance notation into movement and use description/notation to record dance phrases.

570DC450DFE701318D2268A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast two or more dance works and define the choreographic tools being used in each.

570D6B70DFE701318D2168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the following partnering skills: creating contrasting and complementary shapes and receiving and supporting small amounts of weight.

570D0C20DFE701318D2068A86D17958E.description: Work alone, with a partner, or in a small group during the choreographic process.

570CB530DFE701318D1F68A86D17958E.description: Create original dance phrases or brief movement studies that demonstrate the principles of contrast and transition.

570C5F60DFE701318D1E68A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate the structures or forms of AB, ABA, canon, call and response, and narrative.

570C1220DFE701318D1D68A86D17958E.description: Create variations on an original phrase by using a variety of processes (for example, fragmentation, augmentation, diminution, transposition, reordering, chance).

570BC3C0DFE701318D1C68A86D17958E.description: Use improvisation to generate movement and perform brief compositions based on a variety of stimuli (for example, sensory cues, ideas, moods).

570B5FF0DFE701318D1B68A86D17958E.description: The student will implement choreographic principles, processes, and structures.

570A8720DFE701318D1968A86D17958E.description: Continue to refine technique through teacher correction, self-evaluation, and peer evaluation.

570A3B10DFE701318D1868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and use correct dance vocabulary to describe the actions (for example, skip, gallop, swing, bend) and movement elements (for example, levels, direction) in a brief movement study.

5709EE80DFE701318D1768A86D17958E.description: Learn, commit to memory, and replicate sections of a dance work or entire works created by him- or herself and by others.

57099F70DFE701318D1668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate increasing kinesthetic awareness, concentration, focus, and projection in performing movement sequences.

57094A10DFE701318D1568A86D17958E.description: Perform movement sequences with a broad range of movement qualities.

5708F580DFE701318D1468A86D17958E.description: Form shapes and create designs with his or her body and in relation to others' bodies, using a variety of spatial directions, pathways, and levels.

570895D0DFE701318D1368A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate complex dance steps, positions, and patterns in two or more genres or forms of dance.

57083830DFE701318D1268A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate increasingly complex movement sequences from codified dance techniques and kinesthetic skills (for example, alignment, balance, articulation of isolated body parts, elevation and landing, initiation of movement, weight shift, fall and recovery, contraction and release).

5707DD30DFE701318D1168A86D17958E.description: The student will identify and demonstrate movement elements and skills and apply them while performing dance.

document.title: South Carolina Science Academic Standards

6510E9D0DFE70131A2D968A86D17958E.description: Explain how a change of force or a change in mass affects the motion of an object.

6510A5B0DFE70131A2D868A86D17958E.description: Use a graph to illustrate the motion of an object.

651061B0DFE70131A2D768A86D17958E.description: Explain ways to change the effect that friction has on the motion of objects (including changing the texture of the surfaces, changing the amount of surface area involved, and adding lubrication).

65101930DFE70131A2D668A86D17958E.description: Explain how unbalanced forces affect the rate and direction of motion in objects.

650FC8C0DFE70131A2D568A86D17958E.description: Summarize the motion of an object in terms of position, direction, and speed.

650F76E0DFE70131A2D468A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the affects of force (including magnetism, gravity, and friction) on motion.

650EF5F0DFE70131A2D368A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of the nature of force and motion. (Physical Science)

650E5CF0DFE70131A2D168A86D17958E.description: Explain how the mixing and dissolving of foreign substances is related to the pollution of the water, air, and soil

650E1E70DFE70131A2D068A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the fact that when some substances are mixed together, they chemically combine to form a new substance that cannot easily be separated.

650DDE10DFE70131A2CF68A86D17958E.description: Explain how temperature change, particle size, and stirring affect the rate of dissolving.

650D9900DFE70131A2CE68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the solute and the solvent in a solution determine the concentration. .

650D4B50DFE70131A2CD68A86D17958E.description: Use the processes of filtration, sifting, magnetic attraction, evaporation, chromatography, and floatation to separate mixtures.

650D0A40DFE70131A2CC68A86D17958E.description: Summarize the characteristics of a mixture, recognizing a solution as a kind of mixture.

650CC860DFE70131A2CB68A86D17958E.description: Compare the physical properties of the states of matter (including volume, shape, and the movement and spacing of particles).

650C85F0DFE70131A2CA68A86D17958E.description: Recall that matter is made up of particles too small to be seen.

650C42B0DFE70131A2C968A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of properties of matter. (Physical Science)

650BABF0DFE70131A2C768A86D17958E.description: Explain how human activity (including conservation efforts and pollution) has affected the land and the oceans of Earth.

650B68B0DFE70131A2C668A86D17958E.description: Compare the movement of water by waves, currents, and tides.

650B24B0DFE70131A2C568A86D17958E.description: Explain how waves, currents, tides, and storms affect the geologic features of the ocean shore zone (including beaches, barrier islands, estuaries, and inlets).

650A8100DFE70131A2C368A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the geologic landforms of the ocean floor (including the continental shelf and slope, the mid-ocean ridge, rift zone, trench, and the ocean basin).

650A29D0DFE70131A2C268A86D17958E.description: Explain how natural processes (including weathering, erosion, deposition, landslides, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and floods) affect Earth's oceans and land in constructive and destructive ways.

6509D840DFE70131A2C168A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of features, processes, and changes in Earth's land and oceans. (Earth Science)

65094F50DFE70131A2BF68A86D17958E.description: Explain how limiting factors (including food, water, space, and shelter) affect populations in ecosystems.

65090840DFE70131A2BE68A86D17958E.description: Identify the roles of organisms as they interact and depend on one another through food chains and food webs in an ecosystem, considering producers and consumers (herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores), decomposers (microorganisms, termites, worms, and fungi), predators and prey, and parasites and hosts.

6508C470DFE70131A2BD68A86D17958E.description: Compare the characteristics of different ecosystems (including estuaries/salt marshes, oceans, lakes and ponds, forests, and grasslands).

65087CB0DFE70131A2BC68A86D17958E.description: Summarize the composition of an ecosystem, considering both biotic factors (including populations to the level of microorganisms and communities) and abiotic factors.

65082920DFE70131A2BB68A86D17958E.description: Recall the cell as the smallest unit of life and identify its major structures (including cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, and vacuole).

6507E8E0DFE70131A2BA68A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of relationships among biotic and abiotic factors within terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. (Life Science)

65074E80DFE70131A2B868A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate safety procedures when conducting investigations.

65070D60DFE70131A2B768A86D17958E.description: Use a simple technological design process to develop a solution or a product, communicating the design by using descriptions, models, and drawings.

6506C990DFE70131A2B668A86D17958E.description: Evaluate results of an investigation to formulate a valid conclusion based on evidence and communicate the findings of the evaluation in oral or written form.

65067960DFE70131A2B568A86D17958E.description: Construct a line graph from recorded data with correct placement of independent (manipulated) and dependent (responding) variables.

65063290DFE70131A2B468A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate tools and instruments (including a timing device and a 10x magnifier) safely and accurately when conducting a controlled scientific investigation.

6505F2E0DFE70131A2B368A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct controlled scientific investigations, manipulating one variable at a time.

6505AFB0DFE70131A2B268A86D17958E.description: Identify independent (manipulated), dependent (responding), and controlled variables in an experiment.

65056A80DFE70131A2B168A86D17958E.description: Identify questions suitable for generating a hypothesis.

650524F0DFE70131A2B068A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of scientific inquiry, including the foundations of technological design and the processes, skills, and mathematical thinking necessary to conduct a controlled scientific investigation.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

617C6FB0DFE701319D2B68A86D17958E.description: Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

617C1C40DFE701319D2A68A86D17958E.description: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.

617BC9F0DFE701319D2968A86D17958E.description: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.

617B3820DFE701319D2768A86D17958E.description: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by:

617AF490DFE701319D2668A86D17958E.description: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.

617A60F0DFE701319D2468A86D17958E.description: Recognize that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.

617A0370DFE701319D2368A86D17958E.description: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.

comments: For example, "How old am I?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the students in my school?" is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students' ages.
6179B150DFE701319D2268A86D17958E.description: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.

6178E8A0DFE701319D1F68A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another; write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.
comments: For example, in a problem involving motion at constant speed, list and graph ordered pairs of distances and times, and write the equation d = 65t to represent the relationship between distance and time.

6178A1E0DFE701319D1E68A86D17958E.description: Represent and analyze quantitative relationships between dependent and independent variables.

61785130DFE701319D1D68A86D17958E.description: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.

6177EBE0DFE701319D1C68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + p = q and px = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.

6177A1B0DFE701319D1B68A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.

617756B0DFE701319D1A68A86D17958E.description: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.

6176F0F0DFE701319D1968A86D17958E.description: Reason about and solve one-variable equations and inequalities.

61769C70DFE701319D1868A86D17958E.description: Identify when two expressions are equivalent (i.e., when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them).
comments: For example, the expressions y + y + y and 3y are equivalent because they name the same number regardless of which number y stands for.

61765410DFE701319D1768A86D17958E.description: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
comments: For example, apply the distributive property to the expression 3 (2 + x) to produce the equivalent expression 6 + 3x; apply the distributive property to the expression 24x + 18y to produce the equivalent expression 6 (4x + 3y); apply properties of operations to y + y + y to produce the equivalent expression 3y.

617610C0DFE701319D1668A86D17958E.description: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole-number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).
comments: For example, use the formulas V = s³ and A = 6 s² to find the volume and surface area of a cube with sides of length s = 1/2.
For example, describe the expression 2 (8 + 7) as a product of two factors; view (8 + 7) as both a single entity and a sum of two terms.
6175CDE0DFE701319D1568A86D17958E.description: Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.

617589C0DFE701319D1468A86D17958E.description: Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.
comments: For example, express the calculation "Subtract y from 5" as 5 - y.

61754190DFE701319D1368A86D17958E.description: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers.

6174F3C0DFE701319D1268A86D17958E.description: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.

6174A4E0DFE701319D1168A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.

61741220DFE701319D0F68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.

comments: For example, recognize that an account balance less than -30 dollars represents a debt greater than 30 dollars.
6173CE70DFE701319D0E68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.

61738780DFE701319D0D68A86D17958E.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation.
comments: For example, for an account balance of -30 dollars, write |-30| = 30 to describe the size of the debt in dollars.

617334A0DFE701319D0C68A86D17958E.description: Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.
comments: For example, write -3 °C > -7 °C to express the fact that -3 °C is warmer than -7 °C.

6172EF80DFE701319D0B68A86D17958E.description: Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line diagram.
comments: For example, interpret -3 > -7 as a statement that -3 is located to the right of -7 on a number line oriented from left to right.

6172A6F0DFE701319D0A68A86D17958E.description: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers.

61725FD0DFE701319D0968A86D17958E.description: Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.

61720FA0DFE701319D0868A86D17958E.description: Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes.

6171BEC0DFE701319D0768A86D17958E.description: Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., -(-3) = 3, and that 0 is its own opposite.

61715F40DFE701319D0668A86D17958E.description: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number line diagrams and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates.

61711550DFE701319D0568A86D17958E.description: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (e.g., temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of 0 in each situation.

6170C1D0DFE701319D0468A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.

617078D0DFE701319D0368A86D17958E.description: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1—100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.
comments: For example, express 36 + 8 as 4 (9 + 2).

61703370DFE701319D0268A86D17958E.description: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.

616FEC10DFE701319D0168A86D17958E.description: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.

616F9AA0DFE701319D0068A86D17958E.description: Compute fluently with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.

comments: For example, create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (3/4) and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient; use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3. (In general, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.) How much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 3/4-cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length 3/4 mi and area 1/2 square mi?
616F4DE0DFE701319CFF68A86D17958E.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

616EFD10DFE701319CFE68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to divide fractions by fractions.

616E7600DFE701319CFC68A86D17958E.description: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.

616E31B0DFE701319CFB68A86D17958E.description: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (e.g., 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent.

616DE1C0DFE701319CFA68A86D17958E.description: Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.
comments: For example, if it took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns, then at that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate were lawns being mowed?

616D9CD0DFE701319CF968A86D17958E.description: Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios.

616D56B0DFE701319CF868A86D17958E.description: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.

616D0B00DFE701319CF768A86D17958E.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.
comments: Expectations for unit rates in this grade are limited to non-complex fractions.
For example, "This recipe has a ratio of 3 cups of flour to 4 cups of sugar, so there is 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar." "We paid $75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of $5 per hamburger."

For example, "The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak." "For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes."
616CC170DFE701319CF668A86D17958E.description: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.

616C73D0DFE701319CF568A86D17958E.description: Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.

616BED50DFE701319CF368A86D17958E.description: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

616BAA80DFE701319CF268A86D17958E.description: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

616B6530DFE701319CF168A86D17958E.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas V = l w h and V = b h to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

616B1F30DFE701319CF068A86D17958E.description: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

616AD870DFE701319CEF68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.

616A2E60DFE701319CED68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
6169CA30DFE701319CEC68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

616853A0DFE701319CE868A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

5657F3B0DFE701318BFF68A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe applications of technology and documentation in the field of dance (for example, technical production, dance notation, research, choreography, reconstruction of historical dance works).

56573F10DFE701318BFD68A86D17958E.description: Explore movement and create a brief movement phrase based on a concept or idea from another discipline or everyday life (for example, the water cycle).

5656BEA0DFE701318BFB68A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe similarities and differences among the arts.

5655FD60DFE701318BF868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate warm-up exercises and explain the ways that warming up prepares the body for dancing.

5655B4B0DFE701318BF768A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe the ways that dance promotes strength, health, physical safety, and reduced risk of injury.

56556670DFE701318BF668A86D17958E.description: Recognize the ways that healthy practices enhance one's ability to dance, demonstrating respect for his or her own physical well-being and that of others

56548F80DFE701318BF368A86D17958E.description: Observe and/or perform brief movement sequences from masterworks (with all copyright restrictions observed).

56544210DFE701318BF268A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the works of past and present notable figures in dance.

5653F720DFE701318BF168A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the cultural and historical context of dance in different communities and cultures.

5653AD60DFE701318BF068A86D17958E.description: Perform two or more simple folk dances, social dances, classical dances, and/or theatrical dances from a variety of cultures and identify and describe the similarities and differences among them.

56536D30DFE701318BEF68A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of dance in various cultures and historical periods.

5652EE80DFE701318BED68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate appropriate audience behavior while watching and responding to live or recorded dance performances.

5652ACD0DFE701318BEC68A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe aesthetic criteria within dances (for example, skill of the performers, originality of the choreography, intent of the choreographer).

56526710DFE701318BEB68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast two very different dance compositions in terms of space (for example, shape, pathways), time (for example, rhythm, tempo), and/or force/energy/movement qualities (for example, weight, flow).

56521F30DFE701318BEA68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate multiple solutions to a complex movement problem (for example, moving through space in a curved pathway while changing levels) and identify the most interesting solutions.

5651CD60DFE701318BE968A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate and apply critical, creative, and analytic thinking in response to dance.

565143D0DFE701318BE768A86D17958E.description: Explore and perform dances and create brief movement sequences that communicate feelings and ideas.

56510080DFE701318BE668A86D17958E.description: Explain the manner in which lighting, costuming, props, and other scenic elements can contribute to the meaning of a dance.

5650BD90DFE701318BE568A86D17958E.description: Respond to the accompaniment in a dance and identify the mood it creates (for example, sound, music, spoken text).

56506160DFE701318BE468A86D17958E.description: Respond to and interpret dance using dance terminology (for example, movement vocabulary, descriptive language, dance notation, dance elements)

56500D60DFE701318BE368A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate the difference between literal and abstract gestures.

564FAB40DFE701318BE268A86D17958E.description: The student will use dance as a medium to communicate meaning and/or artistic intent.

564F1400DFE701318BE068A86D17958E.description: Use motif description/dance notation to create and record brief dance phrases.

564EB770DFE701318BDF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze and describe the choreographic tools used in major dance works and in those of his or her peers.

564E6AC0DFE701318BDE68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the following partnering skills: creating contrasting and complementary shapes and receiving and supporting small amounts of weight.

564E2D60DFE701318BDD68A86D17958E.description: Work alone, with a partner, or in a small group during the choreographic process.

564DEFD0DFE701318BDC68A86D17958E.description: Explore and demonstrate the principles of contrast and transition.

564DB1A0DFE701318BDB68A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate the structures or forms of AB, ABA, canon, call and response, and narrative.

564D71C0DFE701318BDA68A86D17958E.description: Create a dance sequence, repeat it, and then vary it by making changes in the time, space, and/or force/energy.

564D30F0DFE701318BD968A86D17958E.description: Use movement exploration to discover, compose, and perform solutions to movement problems based on a variety of stimuli (for example, sensory cues, ideas, moods).

564CE330DFE701318BD868A86D17958E.description: The student will implement choreographic principles, processes, and structures.

564C5BA0DFE701318BD668A86D17958E.description: Continue to refine technique through teacher correction and self-evaluation.

564C1DA0DFE701318BD568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and use correct dance vocabulary to describe the actions (for example, skip, gallop, swing, bend) and movement elements (for example, levels, direction) in a brief movement study.

564BDF60DFE701318BD468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate accurate memorization and replication of brief movement sequences.

564B9E60DFE701318BD368A86D17958E.description: Develop and demonstrate increasing kinesthetic awareness, concentration, focus, and projection when performing movement skills.

564B57D0DFE701318BD268A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate a range of movement qualities (for example, sharp, smooth, swinging, shaking, loose).

564B1190DFE701318BD168A86D17958E.description: Safely maintain personal space while moving.

564AD240DFE701318BD068A86D17958E.description: Explore transitions between shapes formed on low, middle, and high levels.

564A9120DFE701318BCF68A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate basic dance steps, positions, and patterns in two or more genres or forms of dance.

564A4970DFE701318BCE68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate a developing sense of strength, range of motion, agility. and coordination in locomotor and nonlocomotor movements.

5649F9B0DFE701318BCD68A86D17958E.description: The student will identify and demonstrate movement elements and skills and apply them while performing dance.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

607FF5F0DFE701319BEE68A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

607F94F0DFE701319BED68A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

607F48A0DFE701319BEC68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

607F0890DFE701319BEB68A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

607E7E70DFE701319BE968A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

607DED70DFE701319BE768A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

607D5A40DFE701319BE568A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

607D0EF0DFE701319BE468A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

607CAD10DFE701319BE368A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

607C22D0DFE701319BE168A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

607BDEB0DFE701319BE068A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

607B9680DFE701319BDF68A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

607B5330DFE701319BDE68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

607B09A0DFE701319BDD68A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

607ABD30DFE701319BDC68A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

607A78E0DFE701319BDB68A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

607A29A0DFE701319BDA68A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

6079DBC0DFE701319BD968A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

60794DD0DFE701319BD768A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

6078CFB0DFE701319BD568A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

60788E80DFE701319BD468A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

60784D40DFE701319BD368A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

60780CC0DFE701319BD268A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

6077C530DFE701319BD168A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

60777760DFE701319BD068A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
6076F810DFE701319BCE68A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.

comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)
6076B540DFE701319BCD68A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.

60767360DFE701319BCC68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

60762FB0DFE701319BCB68A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

6075E2F0DFE701319BCA68A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

60758B70DFE701319BC968A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

6074DA80DFE701319BC768A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

60747DC0DFE701319BC668A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

60731490DFE701319BC268A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

60728100DFE701319BC068A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

62DB3DC0DFE701319F9C68A86D17958E.description: Understand when the probability of an event is 0 or 1.

62CD1150DFE701319F7368A86D17958E.description: Understand fractions as parts of a whole.
