document.title: South Carolina Academic Standards and Performance Indicators for Science

D9AD4F734A9E4F3480CA15A1D742F0DE.description: Design and test solutions that improve the efficiency of a machine by reducing the input energy (effort) or the amount of energy transferred to the surrounding environment as it moves an object.

785E44C773184D3185E542026D1EBD3D.description: Plan and conduct controlled scientific investigations to provide evidence for how the design of simple machines (including levers, pulleys, inclined planes) helps transfer mechanical energy by reducing the amount of force required to do work.

A0C3B592B4E544A48F417A51885CB675.description: Energy transfer occurs when two objects interact thereby exerting force on each other. It is the property of an object or a system that enables it to do work (force moving an object over a distance). Machines are governed by this application of energy, work, and conservation of energy.

7A4803D80E4D439595F9FDC89EBF9F40.description: Design and test devices that minimize or maximize heat transfer by conduction, convection, or radiation.

CC412BB4C5ED429AB1D5A01FD9AA5F7B.description: Develop and use models to describe and compare the directional transfer of heat through convection, radiation, and conduction.

61EAAC753584443E891433E25EAE58C2.description: Develop and use models to exemplify how magnetic fields produced by electrical energy flow in a circuit is interrelated in electromagnets, generators, and simple electrical motors.

6C82972EDD9C419B851838833943C645.description: Construct explanations for how energy is conserved as it is transferred and transformed in electrical circuits.

660C1B83D54B432B80DD05E641EE99E9.description: Develop and use models to exemplify the conservation of energy as it is transformed from kinetic to potential (gravitational and elastic) and vice versa.

79A1C6514D8B44F190B00C70ECCD01A9.description: Analyze and interpret data to describe the properties and compare sources of different forms of energy (including mechanical, electrical, chemical, radiant, and thermal).

A536DCB380D44772A8D4B0137D979206.description: Energy manifests itself in multiple forms, such as mechanical (kinetic energy and potential energy), electrical, chemical, radiant (solar), and thermal energy. According to the principle of conservation of energy, energy cannot be created nor destroyed, but it can be transferred from one place to another and transformed between systems.

0CB05826B88144058203AA7CED382E5F.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of the properties of energy, the transfer and conservation of energy, and the relationship between energy and forces.

18B18F53805F402C915E6D3485A905D1.description: Physical Science: Energy Transfer and Conservation

2A1B30D54D1C452A8B8246F6DD960AE1.description: Construct explanations for how climate is determined in an area (including latitude, elevation, shape of the land, distance from water, global winds, and ocean currents).

9F21EE04498840E8BB24E8461A97E41B.description: Develop and use models to represent how solar energy and convection impact Earth's weather patterns and climate conditions (including global winds, the jet stream, and ocean currents).

3D0F50D9906145428352FDD8D0CA171D.description: Develop and use models to explain how relationships between the movement and interactions of air masses, high and low pressure systems, and frontal boundaries result in weather conditions and storms (including thunderstorms, hurricanes and tornadoes).

7900F8F8CDD849808766E9B5A339C514.description: Analyze and interpret data from weather conditions (including wind speed and direction, air temperature, humidity, cloud types, and air pressure), weather maps, satellites, and radar to predict local weather patterns and conditions.

2D95267ADEEB420FB6402EF151A0135F.description: The complex patterns of changes and movement of water in the atmosphere determined by winds, landforms, ocean temperatures and currents, and convection are major determinants of local weather patterns and climate. Technology has enhanced our ability to measure and predict weather patterns.

A0A9FCE54C81483D8FBB7543AC923E00.description: Construct explanations of the processes involved in the cycling of water through Earth's systems (including transpiration, evaporation, condensation and crystallization, precipitation, and downhill flow of water on land).

8C797D5D88F140E1AF9FBA90021DF1E1.description: Critically analyze scientific arguments based on evidence for and against how different phenomena (natural and human induced) may contribute to the composition of Earth's atmosphere.

24A1864B55FB4A129E731A94E26FB4FE.description: Develop and use models to exemplify the properties of the atmosphere (including the gases, temperature and pressure differences, and altitude changes) and the relative scale in relation to the size of Earth.

BCE326ACDF72483593C23D0AB4275029.description: Earth's atmosphere, an envelope of gases that surround the planet, makes conditions on Earth suitable for living things and influences weather. Water is always moving between the atmosphere (troposphere) and the surface of Earth as a result of the force of gravity and energy from the Sun. The Sun is the driving energy source for heating Earth and for the circulation of Earth's atmosphere.

0C6F5BBC345348BBA30C67D2ADF63CB4.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of the interactions within Earth's systems (flow of energy) that regulate weather and climate.

50015799DE854350849169C42E9507F0.description: Earth Science: Earth's Weather and Climate

BC38ECD62EE646EB87AD63D5E8ABBEF0.description: Analyze and interpret data to describe how plants respond to external stimuli (including temperature, light, touch, water, and gravity).

F44CA105311645428B182096D92B3D1C.description: Plan and conduct controlled scientific investigations to determine how changes in environmental factors (such as air, water, light, minerals, or space) affect the growth and development of a flowering plant.

E1D484DEF0FF45A088BB2E6B2A47135F.description: Develop and use models to compare structural adaptations and processes that flowering plants use for defense, survival and reproduction.

4E183AFF7E834B42A315D911DD90626F.description: Analyze and interpret data to explain how the processes of photosynthesis, respiration, and transpiration work together to meet the needs of plants.

01EE434DD7F0471BB26264DF440ACF1C.description: Construct explanations of how the internal structures of vascular and nonvascular plants transport food and water.

9C87B0D81B224490A906122427DAD2D2.description: The Plant Kingdom consists of organisms that primarily make their own food (autotrophs) and are commonly classified based on internal structures that function in the transport of food and water. Plants have structural and behavioral adaptations that increase the chances of reproduction and survival in changing environments.

271965CF1B2F40EFBFDA86AE7CB082A3.description: Analyze and interpret data to describe how fungi respond to external stimuli (including temperature, light, touch, water, and gravity).

CFC5CD60FB984DD78E88548A947B3AC9.description: Analyze and interpret data from observations to compare how the structures of protists (including euglena, paramecium, and amoeba) and fungi allow them to obtain energy and explore their environment.

DDB02BEC2B72497FBA84882AAA952102.description: The Protist Kingdom is one of the most diverse groups and includes organisms that have characteristics similar to but are not classified as plants, animals, or fungi. These microorganisms live in moist environments and vary in how they obtain energy and move. The Fungi Kingdom consists of organisms that do not make their own food (heterotrophs) but obtain their nutrition through external absorption. Fungi can be grouped by their growth habit or fruiting structure and respond to changes in the environmental stimuli similar to plants.

2C24476398F44E5FA3BD64B0AF5ED0A7.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of the structures, processes, and responses that allow protists, fungi, and plants to survive and reproduce.

A0B979EB681647B88B62781E6A9E3DFF.description: Life Science: Diversity of Life - Protists, Fungi and Plants

F903368356C74A6DB18916D8244B32B5.description: Analyze and interpret data to compare how endothermic and ectothermic animals respond to changes in environmental temperature.

FC93E2FEEE844F1CAB10C613BDAB0C29.description: Obtain and communicate information to compare and classify innate and learned behaviors in animals.

A986B800DC0D463E8121F0ABD95AD6DB.description: Construct explanations of how animal responses (including hibernation, migration, grouping, and courtship) to environmental stimuli allow them to survive and reproduce.

8E827ABCD2174369A5F20EB70A26AB71.description: Obtain and communicate information to explain how the structural adaptations and processes of animals allow for defense, movement, or resource obtainment.

4A1391DC759C447DBD7C1DDB76EB5278.description: Analyze and interpret data related to the diversity of animals to support claims that all animals (vertebrates and invertebrates) share common characteristics.

F1DD6FBE0F334871810F909363296151.description: The Animal Kingdom includes a diversity of organisms that have many characteristics in common. Classification of animals is based on structures that function in growth, reproduction, and survival. Animals have both structural and behavioral adaptations that increase the chances of reproduction and survival in changing environments.

BB2A675A84944192BA685399301B034A.description: Develop and use models to classify organisms based on the current hierarchical taxonomic structure (including the kingdoms of protists, plants, fungi, and animals).

315DDBA658C2424DA13B6BA9B2DCF049.description: Obtain and communicate information to support claims that living organisms (1) obtain and use resources for energy, (2) respond to stimuli, (3) reproduce, and (4) grow and develop.

D6CC4F7A09CA45DFB9C4305295966E35.description: Life is the quality that differentiates living things (organisms) from nonliving objects or those that were once living. All organisms are made up of cells, need food and water, a way to dispose of waste, and an environment in which they can live. Because of the diversity of life on Earth, scientists have developed a way to organize groups of organisms according to their characteristic traits, making it easier to identify and study them.

219C63516F8C4F20992C7A1911B747CC.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of how scientists classify organisms and how the structures, processes, behaviors, and adaptations of animals allow them to survive.

DD3ADB43B45846D889ACE4E78B402ABA.description: Life Science: Diversity of Life - Classification and Animals

8244ECF1BA204F2883133D1B408EB5E4.description: Construct devices or design solutions using scientific knowledge to solve specific problems or needs: (1) ask questions to identify problems or needs, (2) ask questions about the criteria and constraints of the device or solutions, (3) generate and communicate ideas for possible devices or solutions, (4) build and test devices or solutions, (5) determine if the devices or solutions solved the problem and refine the design if needed, and (6) communicate the results.

156C0EAE7DE7445C9D2DEE78FA938F2A.description: Technology is any modification to the natural world created to fulfill the wants and needs of humans. The engineering design process involves a series of iterative steps used to solve a problem and often leads to the development of a new or improved technology.

C4F0B3331EFF40599FCB054598F16950.description: Obtain and evaluate scientific information to (1) answer questions, (2) explain or describe phenomena, (3) develop models, (4) evaluate hypotheses, explanations, claims, or designs or (5) identify and/or fill gaps in knowledge. Communicate using the conventions and expectations of scientific writing or oral presentations by (1) evaluating grade-appropriate primary or secondary scientific literature, or (2) reporting the results of student experimental investigations.

9E73307F90194D9093D9A21827FBF086.description: Construct and analyze scientific arguments to support claims, explanations, or designs using evidence from observations, data, or informational texts.

3B0813CD73394AC8820594FCC3EADDCB.description: Construct explanations of phenomena using (1) primary or secondary scientific evidence and models, (2) conclusions from scientific investigations, (3) predictions based on observations and measurements, or (4) data communicated in graphs, tables, or diagrams

6C4AE619C9E344A2961B3529C9BEAB16.description: Use mathematical and computational thinking to (1) use and manipulate appropriate metric units, (2) collect and analyze data, (3) express relationships between variables for models and investigations, or (4) use grade-level appropriate statistics to analyze data.

57065D51279345E0A34E8AD80A0F892F.description: Analyze and interpret data from informational texts, observations, measurements, or investigations using a range of methods (such as tabulation, graphing, or statistical analysis) to (1) reveal patterns and construct meaning or (2) support hypotheses, explanations, claims, or designs.

2F0C0D7DDA01401AAD3A2DC04FC32104.description: Plan and conduct controlled scientific investigations to answer questions, test hypotheses, and develop explanations: (1) formulate scientific questions and testable hypotheses, (2) identify materials, procedures, and variables, (3) select and use appropriate tools or instruments to collect qualitative and quantitative data, and (4) record and represent data in an appropriate form. Use appropriate safety procedures.

3665E8C5C61740C0BE9087459DF8D8D9.description: Develop, use, and refine models to (1) understand or represent phenomena, processes, and relationships, (2) test devices or solutions, or (3) communicate ideas to others.

5149B5BADB724CDCA3818C2CB1DB045C.description: Ask questions to (1) generate hypotheses for scientific investigations, (2) refine models, explanations, or designs, or (3) extend the results of investigations or challenge claims.

1F65BEEC66FA4382AA184B9A386C1425.description: The practices of science and engineering support the development of science concepts, develop the habits of mind that are necessary for scientific thinking, and allow students to engage in science in ways that are similar to those used by scientists and engineers.

9900530D194C4F6DA5F7A4629EE96D15.description: The student will use the science and engineering practices, including the processes and skills of scientific inquiry, to develop understandings of science content.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

6153E010DFE701319CE368A86D17958E.description: Solve real world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, how much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 1/3-cup servings are in 2 cups of raisins?

61539350DFE701319CE268A86D17958E.description: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for 4 ÷ (1/5), and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.

For example, create a story context for (1/3) ÷ 4, and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 because (1/12) × 4 = 1/3.
61534270DFE701319CE168A86D17958E.description: Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number, and compute such quotients.

6152FA40DFE701319CE068A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.
comments: Students able to multiply fractions in general can develop strategies to divide fractions in general, by reasoning about the relationship between multiplication and division. But division of a fraction by a fraction is not a requirement at this grade

6152B6B0DFE701319CDF68A86D17958E.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

61526D20DFE701319CDE68A86D17958E.description: Explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than 1 as a familiar case); explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than 1 results in a product smaller than the given number; and relating the principle of fraction equivalence a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) to the effect of multiplying a/b by 1.

61522020DFE701319CDD68A86D17958E.description: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.

615194D0DFE701319CDB68A86D17958E.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.

615145B0DFE701319CDA68A86D17958E.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)

6150E410DFE701319CD968A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.

61509310DFE701319CD868A86D17958E.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, interpret 3/4 as the result of dividing 3 by 4, noting that 3/4 multiplied by 4 equals 3, and that when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

61502D90DFE701319CD768A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.

comments: For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 < 1/2.
614FE8F0DFE701319CD668A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.

614FA570DFE701319CD568A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
comments: For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.)

614F6420DFE701319CD468A86D17958E.description: Use equivalent fractions as a strategy to add and subtract fractions.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

614ED830DFE701319CD268A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

614E9060DFE701319CD168A86D17958E.description: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category.
comments: For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.

614E3F20DFE701319CD068A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.

614DF1F0DFE701319CCF68A86D17958E.description: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.

614D8640DFE701319CCE68A86D17958E.description: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the 0 on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., x-axis and x-coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).

614D34B0DFE701319CCD68A86D17958E.description: Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

614CA770DFE701319CCB68A86D17958E.description: Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

614C5420DFE701319CCA68A86D17958E.description: Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.

614C1480DFE701319CC968A86D17958E.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole-number products as volumes, e.g., to represent the associative property of multiplication.

614BD090DFE701319CC868A86D17958E.description: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.

614B8AD0DFE701319CC768A86D17958E.description: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, and improvised units.

614B45B0DFE701319CC668A86D17958E.description: A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units.

614AEFE0DFE701319CC568A86D17958E.description: A cube with side length 1 unit, called a "unit cube," is said to have "one cubic unit" of volume, and can be used to measure volume.

614AACE0DFE701319CC468A86D17958E.description: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.

614A6CE0DFE701319CC368A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of volume and relate volume to multiplication and to addition.

614A2870DFE701319CC268A86D17958E.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real world problems.

6149E400DFE701319CC168A86D17958E.description: Convert like measurement units within a given measurement system.

61499C30DFE701319CC068A86D17958E.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.

614895F0DFE701319CBD68A86D17958E.description: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

61484840DFE701319CBC68A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

6147F160DFE701319CBB68A86D17958E.description: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

6147AAA0DFE701319CBA68A86D17958E.description: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.

614762A0DFE701319CB968A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.

61471560DFE701319CB868A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

6146D330DFE701319CB768A86D17958E.description: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., 347.392 = 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 × 1 + 3 × (1/10) + 9 × (1/100) + 2 × (1/1000).

614691F0DFE701319CB668A86D17958E.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths.

61464D90DFE701319CB568A86D17958E.description: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.

61460690DFE701319CB468A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.

614563F0DFE701319CB268A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 0, and given the rule "Add 6" and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.
61451AB0DFE701319CB168A86D17958E.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane.

61449360DFE701319CAF68A86D17958E.description: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them.
comments: For example, express the calculation "add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2" as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.

61444940DFE701319CAE68A86D17958E.description: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.

61434870DFE701319CAB68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

6142F810DFE701319CAA68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

61418D70DFE701319CA668A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

6140EC50DFE701319CA468A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: South Carolina Academic Standards and Performance Indicators for Science

7B972862ADCB4B898DDAAD7CECB4849A.description: Design and test possible devices or solutions that reduce the effects of friction on the motion of an object.

267C9EBF9484446FA1D5D51B679E8123.description: Analyze and interpret data to describe how a change of force, a change in mass, or friction affects the motion of an object.

8A58D2370F364C83AACC5115D241C154.description: Plan and conduct controlled scientific investigations to test the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the rate and direction of motion of objects.

32207348AC744E2694E719B9C64D456E.description: Develop and use models to explain how the amount or type of force (contact and non-contact) affects the motion of an object.

31E3F2144E3D4E10A3CBB0CF533329FB.description: Use mathematical and computational thinking to describe and predict the motion of an object (including position, direction, and speed).

64EF74C49EEF4B79995BBB19D91C5732.description: The motion of an object can be described in terms of its position, direction, and speed. The rate and motion of an object is determined by multiple factors.

F9F4CDD54F374DBB8A203BC9B1DE58FE.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of the factors that affect the motion of an object.

5FFAC871977044AF937AD462AD93F3BE.description: Design and test the appropriate method(s) (such as filtration, sifting, attraction to magnets, evaporation, chromatography, or floatation) for separating various mixtures.

ADA63D90F02F42099889009DC689D148.description: Conduct controlled scientific investigations to test how different variables (including temperature change, particle size, and stirring) affect the rate of dissolving.

9087A758C7DA4DAEA8C5B5EECA0FCBBB.description: Construct explanations for how the amount of solute and the solvent determine the concentration of a solution.

F2FBD4635D1844DBA7FEFF77E929262B.description: Develop models using observations to describe mixtures, including solutions, based on their characteristics.

CB21E729E0764D49862CD048EBCD418F.description: Analyze and interpret data to support claims that when two substances are mixed the total amount (mass) of the substances does not change.

5ED88B8FF8E5413C80660D1616487E6A.description: A mixture is formed when two or more kinds of matter are put together. Sometimes when two or more different substances are mixed together, a new substance with different properties may be formed but the total amount (mass) of the substances is conserved. Solutions are a special type of mixture in which one substance is dissolved evenly into another substance. When the physical properties of the components in a mixture are not changed, they can be separated in different physical ways.

803FA214EF864DC5B418A2217F9BC876.description: Matter is made up of particles that are too small to be seen. Even though the particles are very small, the movement and spacing of these particles determines the basic properties of matter.

63C95D032D054FBB8EBF21A9A20E0BB4.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of the physical properties of matter and mixtures.

708632B979C9445A9AC1C01E0EA47187.description: Define problems caused by natural processes or human activities and test possible solutions to reduce the impact on landforms and the ocean shore zone.

BAA198E50D8B4FF188F97FC89D5D4CB1.description: Construct scientific arguments to support claims that human activities (such as conservation efforts or pollution) affect the land and oceans of Earth.

7D375F1FFF304DDA83A40F8C40340468.description: Develop and use models to explain the effect of the movement of ocean water (including waves, currents, and tides) on the ocean shore zone (including beaches, barrier islands, estuaries, and inlets).

D205DE666A0E4F5C91646689EAA8A9C1.description: Analyze and interpret data to describe and predict how natural processes (such as weathering, erosion, deposition, earthquakes, tsunamis, hurricanes, or storms) affect Earth's surface.

EC417680353A436FA3896402B1EF6322.description: Earth's oceans and landforms can be affected by natural processes in various ways. Humans cannot eliminate natural hazards caused by these processes but can take steps to reduce their impacts. Human activities can affect the land and oceans in positive and negative ways.

20615F06BF384CB0B1E966A4655BB425.description: Develop and use models to describe and compare the characteristics and locations of the landforms on continents with those on the ocean floor (including the continental shelf and slope, the mid-ocean ridge, the rift zone, the trench, and the abyssal plain).

D0C989D6ADA543989164B715F157EDC0.description: Construct explanations of how different landforms and surface features result from the location and movement of water on Earth's surface through watersheds (drainage basins) and rivers.

5BF225473DAA4EA38EA2A4912F201675.description: Some of the land on Earth is located above water and some is located below the oceans. The downhill movement of water as it flows to the ocean shapes the appearance of the land. There are patterns in the location and structure of landforms found on the continents and those found on the ocean floor.

B2541F3A2C5D48998534B14C620BE755.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of how natural processes and human activities affect the features of Earth's landforms and oceans.

BC91B1AEFFCB46ACB68F589FEF22CA98.description: Earth Science: Changes in Landforms and Oceans

779C517B1FC641B1AEE81DFA3B2CE187.description: Construct scientific arguments to explain how limiting factors (including food, water, space, and shelter) or a newly introduced organism can affect an ecosystem.

559C64F36EAC45A688402B7E32E58DDB.description: Construct explanations for how organisms interact with each other in an ecosystem (including predators and prey, and parasites and hosts).

A308CF3791F2447A82DD1A712CA1A229.description: Develop and use models of food chains and food webs to describe the flow of energy in an ecosystem.

B6F2F9867BC74BA0805123EC828B4A1F.description: Analyze and interpret data to explain how organisms obtain their energy and classify an organisms as producers, consumers (including herbivore, carnivore, and omnivore), or decomposers (such as fungi and bacteria).

57F4B3E2AF7F47AC9C5068E319833E6D.description: All organisms need energy to live and grow. Energy is obtained from food. The role an organism serves in an ecosystem can be described by the way in which it gets its energy. Energy is transferred within an ecosystem as organisms produce, consume, or decompose food. A healthy ecosystem is one in which a diversity of life forms are able to meet their needs in a relatively stable web of life.

0257BE660B35418BAF80EB498A528C6B.description: Obtain and communicate information to describe and compare the biotic factors (including individual organisms, populations, and communities) of different terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

A8AE89478E984326942E4DC1A4B83365.description: Analyze and interpret data to summarize the abiotic factors (including quantity of light and water, range of temperature, salinity, and soil composition) of different terrestrial ecosystems and aquatic ecosystems.

97C4DF0C7D664122945654D68D43B24F.description: Ecosystems are complex, interactive systems that include both the living components (biotic factors) and physical components (abiotic factors) of the environment. Ecosystems can be classified as either terrestrial (such as forests, wetlands, and grasslands) or aquatic (such as oceans, estuaries, lakes, and ponds).

F4F5FDAC547445DC84DC11B0854AB3D7.description: The student will demonstrate an understanding of relationships among biotic and abiotic factors within terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

50C361A9358D4A6BBD6E56559EC0B56E.description: Life Science: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems

65C9FA778A6242259F656F7874EC8555.description: Construct devices or design solutions to solve specific problems or needs: (1) ask questions to identify problems or needs, (2) ask questions about the criteria and constraints of the devices or solutions, (3) generate and communicate ideas for possible devices or solutions, (4) build and test devices or solutions, (5) determine if the devices or solutions solved the problem and refine the design if needed, and (6) communicate the results.

A824B8A163A648E1BF7C09BF0B0E84E8.description: Technology is any modification to the natural world created to fulfill the wants and needs of humans. The engineering design process involves a series of iterative steps used to solve a problem and often leads to the development of a new or improved technology.

8B21771A4A7E4438B75ECC127CD4BF05.description: Obtain and evaluate informational texts, observations, data collected, or discussions to (1) generate and answer questions, (2) understand phenomena, (3) develop models, or (4) support hypotheses, explanations, claims, or designs. Communicate observations and explanations using the conventions and expectations of oral and written language.

BD2B9508D0AF46469F47CC5715023BC8.description: Construct scientific arguments to support claims, explanations, or designs using evidence from observations, data, or informational texts.

39410CBCC91E414DA6E8E08D5DD59F8C.description: Construct explanations of phenomena using (1) scientific evidence and models, (2) conclusions from scientific investigations, (3) predictions based on observations and measurements, or (4) data communicated in graphs, tables, or diagrams.

8AB0FB2842704DAE9A1A829CEE6577AF.description: Use mathematical and computational thinking to (1) express quantitative observations using appropriate metric units, (2) collect and analyze data, or (3) understand patterns, trends and relationships between variables.

461F8E4189B141B196747EC1FD769A99.description: Analyze and interpret data from informational texts, observations, measurements, or investigations using a range of methods (such as tabulation or graphing) to (1) reveal patterns and construct meaning or (2) support hypotheses, explanations, claims, or designs.

EC7EA04162CE4BF2836C77045E74C2C2.description: Plan and conduct controlled scientific investigations to answer questions, test hypotheses and predictions, and develop explanations: (1) formulate scientific questions and testable hypotheses, (2) identify materials, procedures, and variables, (3) select and use appropriate tools or instruments to collect qualitative and quantitative data, and (4) record and represent data in an appropriate form. Use appropriate safety procedures.

A4FF9F59C4ED421E82D913039D4681F9.description: Develop, use, and refine models to (1) understand or represent phenomena, processes, and relationships, (2) test devices or solutions, or (3) communicate ideas to others.

C81481A2337645F8BB621345813CB7A3.description: Ask questions used to (1) generate hypotheses for scientific investigations or (2) refine models, explanations, or designs.

F688024E13A74668B12142BB6B40FF48.description: The practices of science and engineering support the development of science concepts, develop the habits of mind that are necessary for scientific thinking, and allow students to engage in science in ways that are similar to those used by scientists and engineers.

DD7F89D3177C4CDBAF33B317A50A82AA.description: The student will use the science and engineering practices, including the processes and skills of scientific inquiry, to develop understandings of science content.

document.title: South Carolina Academic Standards for the Visual and Performing Arts - Media Arts

534AAAF0DFE70131873E68A86D17958E.description: Practice legal and ethical behavior in the media arts and the use of technology.

534A6960DFE70131873D68A86D17958E.description: Explore human, cultural, and societal issues related to the media arts and the use of technology.

534A2510DFE70131873C68A86D17958E.description: The student will demonstrate a knowledge of digital citizenship and a sense of responsibility in the media arts.

534919C0DFE70131873868A86D17958E.description: View and describe a variety of media art forms.

5348D9D0DFE70131873768A86D17958E.description: The student will understand the context and history of the development of the media arts from the late nineteenth century to present and will recognize the role of media artwork in world cultures.

53483C60DFE70131873568A86D17958E.description: Explore the financial aspects of media arts productions, including budget responsibility and career opportunities.

5347F000DFE70131873468A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the media arts with other arts disciplines and other content areas.

5347AB30DFE70131873368A86D17958E.description: Identify uses of the media arts in everyday life.

53476700DFE70131873268A86D17958E.description: The student will make connections between the media arts and other arts disciplines, other content areas, and the world.

5346EA60DFE70131873068A86D17958E.description: Identify creative techniques used in a variety of media texts (for example, television, film, radio, Internet).

5346A370DFE70131872F68A86D17958E.description: Describe ways that different audiences might respond to specific media texts.

53465E50DFE70131872E68A86D17958E.description: Express his or her thoughts and feelings about simple media texts.

53462270DFE70131872D68A86D17958E.description: Identify messages in simple media texts.

5345E5E0DFE70131872C68A86D17958E.description: Identify the purpose and the intended audience for some simple media texts.

5345A7B0DFE70131872B68A86D17958E.description: The student will access, analyze, interpret, and create media texts.

53452910DFE70131872968A86D17958E.description: Design and create media artwork that communicates his or her personal experiences.

5344E4B0DFE70131872868A86D17958E.description: Develop a basic media arts vocabulary and identify elements of artistic design specific to individual media.

53449E50DFE70131872768A86D17958E.description: The student will create media artwork that demonstrates an understanding and command of the principles of artistic design.

53442300DFE70131872568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate an understanding of and respect for the accepted procedures regarding the responsible care of media arts equipment and materials.

5343E400DFE70131872468A86D17958E.description: Use a variety of media technologies, techniques, and processes to communicate ideas.

5343A4C0DFE70131872368A86D17958E.description: Identify the specific skills, knowledge, and abilities necessary for creating media artwork.

534361E0DFE70131872268A86D17958E.description: The student will develop and expand his or her knowledge of the processes, techniques, and applications used in the creation of media artwork.

document.title: South Carolina College- and Career-Ready Standards for Mathematics

5521AD5C000B4BD3AB837313FECE581C.description: Compare and order decimal numbers to hundredths, and justify using concrete and visual models.

38DEE2968FA847A7A90B7D64906D7F1F.description: Write a fraction with a denominator of 10 or 100 using decimal notation, and read and write a decimal number as a fraction.

F9412CF2B75F41CE810A2C8B43DC688A.description: Express a fraction with a denominator of 10 as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of 100 and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators of 10 and 100.

DCEE7B7C066D4A0388C01BD1051C704F.description: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number (i.e., use visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem).

6A68C6BDE2AD49A8A8DEF5723FC191F4.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number;

8FD52A33BA4C41E6B3D916DDC5E1FD8D.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b;

EF9EF946C58F460281E0EA8D052B3AEF.description: Apply and extend an understanding of multiplication by multiplying a whole number and a fraction (i.e., denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 25, 100).

EA55171B1F8C46BD9BC8BFD3FEE8B690.description: Solve real-world problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators.

8F2B6B36C9D84C1EA33721CCCDE11A03.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators;

C107793C2CC0499DA4B05A43215F3A9E.description: Compose and decompose a fraction in more than one way, recording each composition and decomposition as an addition or subtraction equation;

7CD0E30FA5BB4FA5AFCABF0C7C841D8E.description: Develop an understanding of addition and subtraction of fractions (i.e., denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 25, 100) based on unit fractions.

AF3EEB43ABF8469C883EECEFA5BFBAC9.description: Compare two given fractions (i.e., denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 25, 100) by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as ½ and represent the comparison using the symbols >, =, or <.

FBB6CA59679C4029AABDCA0C634DF56A.description: Explain why a fraction (i.e., denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 25, 100), a/b, is equivalent to a fraction, n×a/n×b , by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

8E1EBE2EA4654C038EAADB9301431DDD.description: Determine the value of a collection of coins and bills greater than $1.00.

1D64B3D8F0E0455A856E197B02072D48.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles in real-world and mathematical problems.

9B1DAFB0037C41179628960C5A6306D1.description: Measure and draw angles in whole number degrees using a protractor.

8214E8DBD40D41F7A0AAA945AD773F53.description: Understand the relationship of an angle measurement to a circle.

2CAE20199AD04A4DB43B8B81E89456E4.description: Create a line plot to display a data set (i.e., generated by measuring length to the nearest quarter-inch and eighth-inch) and interpret the line plot.

1FE769CA8D194DC3A990C28D1B95D012.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles.

1782FE88CB51476B82BFE8474A49EEE0.description: Solve real-world problems involving distance/length, intervals of time within 12 hours, liquid volume, mass, and money using the four operations.

F1F30C7F87204E0CB8D6313BA05E2A91.description: Convert measurements within a single system of measurement, customary (i.e., in., ft., yd., oz., lb., sec., min., hr.) or metric (i.e., cm, m, km, g, kg, mL, L) from a larger to a smaller unit.

C98166AEE0854E7AB2935EF19036AE5D.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

73853CC7C44D4C74A5E74D06D5A2AA5D.description: Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

DEC9F53777C640FA915FE090F5B097E1.description: Classify quadrilaterals based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines.

555195AD967E48B89DFF217F6F83277F.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (i.e., right, acute, obtuse), and parallel and perpendicular lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

58648BDA8CA64991931BB0BE69E909E3.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule and determine a term that appears later in the sequence.

929D8D5F14374DCDB9660099F066C4CB.description: Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Find all factors for a whole number in the range 1 – 100 and determine whether the whole number is prime or composite.

4DA1937CC097459E9E47688D48BFE8A4.description: Solve multi-step, real-world problems using the four operations. Represent the problem using an equation with a variable as the unknown quantity.

D76FAF8896A74B8BAB2B93FADFF3D188.description: Solve real-world problems using multiplication (product unknown) and division (group size unknown, number of groups unknown).

7E07F4913A6141C8AFB77D0DEECDFD56.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (e.g. interpret 35 = 5x7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5.) Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

352B9215E60147E49C18CB4B0113EDF0.description: Divide up to a four-digit dividend by a one-digit divisor using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division.

8212C88E12FE4977875D9DF79ECD0095.description: Multiply up to a four-digit number by a one-digit number and multiply a two-digit number by a two-digit number using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using rectangular arrays, area models and/or equations.

67886FE833F445F49D7EC48948BCF027.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using strategies to include a standard algorithm.

1C14E535ADD944B9B602B3E3BB9F413A.description: Use rounding as one form of estimation and round whole numbers to any given place value.

7C2495390BC844B184D27B92780251EC.description: Recognize math periods and number patterns within each period to read and write in standard form large numbers through 999,999,999.

B3229361FC9C48DB9AC7762E475F408B.description: Understand that, in a multi-digit whole number, a digit represents ten times what the same digit represents in the place to its right.

5E43AF712C224FF48E88A42960393A62.description: Look for structures to interpret meaning and develop solution strategies.

9BD71FA96ACD4E0AA353B9AA7D4A7E38.description: Recognize mathematical repetition in order to make generalizations.

1AEC79CFA3F443FDB98CA7CAD1D134B4.description: Recognize complex mathematical objects as being composed of more than one simple object.

71FE37112C1740FC94088F2135DDA0E9.description: Identify and utilize structure and patterns.

1345CAC05064457B9A51E66DD1A809BE.description: Use appropriate units, scales, and labels.

1422EE03EB5547A1930A3686A53D4D98.description: Use appropriate and precise mathematical language.

793AA694989D432DB5AF81718EA0A1D8.description: Represent numbers in an appropriate form according to the context of the situation.

A5C13D04C823456C8D2D3B2AACB8C663.description: Use a variety of mathematical tools effectively and strategically.

34093ED99FD7446783BD620179A31978.description: Evaluate the reasonableness of a model and refine if necessary.

548AE2D35D7E46AEB56FAD9F43BA483D.description: Make assumptions and estimates to simplify complicated situations.

A498837362744DAC96EA961648D211D0.description: Interpret mathematical models in the context of the situation.

2A274F4FE3094115AB1C0C03B5869EF2.description: Identify relevant quantities and develop a model to describe their relationships.

759E5DFC2A42405D8F5CCA1D3786A5C5.description: Connect mathematical ideas and real-world situations through modeling.

FF114499843349D497697B128EB94C58.description: Reflect on and provide thoughtful responses to the reasoning of others.

D12E9DC4CFE74224A05F050D40955931.description: Make conjectures and explore their validity.

A873E80F13244793A0AD79C8806946F1.description: Compare and discuss the validity of various reasoning strategies.

C0684E49301D4EA78C930497CF21FCFB.description: Construct and justify a solution to a problem.

0048FE6975F747EDBE8D4E9DC69C5642.description: Use critical thinking skills to justify mathematical reasoning and critique the reasoning of others.

46FC03ACA8344071BB83A5160566EEFC.description: Connect the meaning of mathematical operations to the context of a given situation.

FF01256512954513ADF7932B9E9B7E0A.description: Make sense of quantities and their relationships in mathematical and real-world situations.

CF912CE52D6D4F85A1ED71A4590DC18F.description: Evaluate the success of an approach to solve a problem and refine it if necessary.

CA1961BA5BD84DA8B73C0140894805B5.description: Relate a problem to prior knowledge.

A160ECA23E7741E28B5ABB35F1B2CC71.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: South Carolina Academic Standards for Health and Safety Education

F02096A6E2054D57A5A8006BE8DD4558.description: Explain ways that peers, family, and community can participate in organ and tissue donations.

FE95C440F5A3442D929EE55BA47CDA6F.description: Advocate for the promotion and protection of a healthy and safe environment, including community, personal, and family environments.

A7C42D8296B34C87B02C2B41875ABB7B.description: Advocate for self and others to increase their level of physical activity.

7ED22A17A87C417183BCF38D85EF13BC.description: Encourage others to choose healthy foods.

8926E3AC33DD4B2F9BAD62FD13805DBE.description: Promote intervention and outreach for those dealing with suicidal intentions or behavioral health problems (e.g., peers, family members).

F36C4AD644D34DD2A9B7D85D2867DE6F.description: Promote intervention and outreach for others dealing with unhealthy relationships.

D88045865D134458A3C1FAE23008A2BD.description: Advocate for safe environments that encourage dignified and respectful treatment of everyone.

E7A9D8EFA8C843E195F6DC3EF3CEB619.description: Advocate for disaster preparedness in the home, school, and community.

E00AA2FD37CC4590837A3C21B53E337C.description: Promote access to valid information and community resources that support abstinence and discourage risky sexual behavior.

75BF7570DDE84E95BB6982EBA43EC7E4.description: Promote intervention and outreach for those dealing with ATOD use or abuse (e.g., peers, family members).

D50D1BA56BE2464BAE5F7CB48EA18536.description: Encourage positive alternatives to ATOD use.

BE9600C4313D4F2D9DD5030F10E196B2.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to advocate for personal, family, and community health.

04D7DA01A1BE48049DAD5AE0DC6EF0CD.description: Implement a long-term personal wellness plan to maintain and improve healthy practices and behaviors.

882EF03C678848C790D7C5B882F0A441.description: Examine the relationship between personal nutritional intake and overall physical, oral, and mental health.

1C41285AB3F14A6F971B1BF1277F091B.description: Implement a wellness plan that meets the current federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans and the federal physical activity guidelines for Americans.

CAB1C58BD91A4028AFFDD4ABF240F569.description: Establish boundaries that promote safety, respect, awareness, and acceptance.

1395CBD768AD49058E0905E4FE62F11A.description: Demonstrate effective strategies for resolving interpersonal conflicts (e.g., end or avoid unhealthy relationships).

6C92735588BC4BCC92E2A1381EF94A8B.description: Demonstrate strategies to develop and maintain a positive self-image.

5FA8039E9DC44FC68F4F8F2E67A17887.description: Implement a plan to increase personal resiliency.

8B865428F24C471EBE9DB90EA4816E00.description: Perform appropriate first aid and other emergency procedures for a given scenario (e.g., CPR, AED).

3F2E4FD4F57B4BC6975BB091CF04D53C.description: Discuss respect for the boundaries of others as they relate to intimacy and sexual behavior.

0CA999827727442FA27C4B7FE311854C.description: Practice strategies for dealing with family, peer, and cultural pressure regarding ATOD (e.g., opioid, prescription drugs, heroin).

9D90DA9E7C0943F28CCA5C65AA566DDF.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to practice health-enhancing behaviors and avoid or reduce health risks.

6A140259BCB74B489406ACC6C1C5D6E9.description: Create a long-term personal health plan that is adaptable to changing health needs based on genetics, family history, and personal health behaviors.

7845498CF39447B79A7A02FF810F1A0D.description: Set a SMART goal to attain the federally recommended levels of physical activity and physical fitness for Americans.

3B2C780289A9461B9DC293ED4FC5380E.description: Set a SMART goal to achieve a healthy eating plan by limiting sugar, fat, and salt consumption.

7E576286E15E4A8496536B4C18DFF04D.description: Review resiliency and develop a personal plan to increase or maintain one's personal resiliency.

FBA98957B0A5443E846874FFB5EE2CCA.description: Develop coping strategies to avoid, manage, and minimize participation in violent activities, including gang involvement.

50F1BC6F986C4585A0CF0DAA9526D3FB.description: Create a plan for communicating personal boundaries as they relate to intimacy and sexual behavior.

D22C392626A843C99B668786776F21FE.description: Set a specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and timely (SMART) goal to maintain reproductive health, including self-exams, and annual appointments with health providers.

C1759020ADD94B73AF910FF19505D798.description: Predict ways that short and long-term goals can be affected by ATOD use.

42AE25DDE077432EB1AD04D5490C5205.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to use goal-setting skills to enhance health.

F1971A16F1F148B6AF873CC25472B405.description: Integrate knowledge of body structure and function to make sound decisions related to personal and community health (e.g., disease prevention, injury prevention, oral health, organ and tissue donation).

075BABE0863242248CE47DCB49BE2821.description: Justify when individual or collaborative decision-making is appropriate.

C67A0D6197754C7B948AD9A714B4E127.description: Utilize the current federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans to compare and contrast food choices on a variety of menus.

1FB610796FB34DD4939DA0FFB5EE3F83.description: Discuss situations that may require professional mental, emotional, and social health services.

4FB8531556304A6F9D3C83D25EB7CB47.description: Recognize the warning signs of anxiety, depression, and suicidal behavior.

F862B815799144E794CF608EF07E4FDF.description: Assess the types of situations when it is necessary to seek help and/or to leave an unhealthy relationship or environment.

B9F811EB12F94CD88DFC3BB5A0E3AED8.description: Explain ways that ATOD affects an individual's thinking and decision-making, and increases the risk of violence and other illegal activities (i.e., opioid, prescription drugs, heroin).

physical (abiotic) factors (such as light, temperature, water, or soil quality). Disruptions to any
component of an ecosystem can lead to shifts in its diversity and abundance of populations.

parental organisms and their offspring. Organisms that reproduce sexually transfer genetic
information (DNA) to their offspring. This transfer of genetic information through inheritance
leads to greater similarity among individuals within a population than between populations.

one or more cells, (2) cells are the basic unit of structure and function of organisms, and
(3) cells come only from existing cells.

organisms are composed of one (unicellular) or many cells (multi-cellular) and require food and
water, a way to dispose of waste, and an environment in which they can live in order to survive.
Through the use of technology, scientists have discovered special structures within individual cells
that have specific functions that allow the cell to grow, survive, and reproduce. Bacteria are one-celled organisms found almost everywhere and can be both helpful and harmful. They can be
simply classified by their size, shape and whether or not they can move.

document.title: South Carolina Biology 1 Standards

8F9BCE7B1D09477CB2C79942264659D4.description:
Design solutions to reduce the impact of human activity on the biodiversity of an
ecosystem.

B206A72339114834959C3E55DAE76F7E.description:
Conceptual Understanding: Sustaining biodiversity maintains ecosystem functioning
and productivity which are essential to supporting and enhancing life on Earth. Humans depend
on the living world for the resources and other benefits provided by biodiversity. Human activity
can impact biodiversity.

DF00235581514631B08300284D5360C1.description:
Construct scientific arguments to support claims that the changes in the biotic and
abiotic components of various ecosystems over time affect the ability of an ecosystem
to maintain homeostasis.

6F7FFC4634E3467CBB92CBC06E571B76.description:
Conceptual Understanding: A complex set of interactions within an ecosystem can
keep its numbers and types of organisms relatively stable over long periods of time. Fluctuations
in conditions can challenge the functioning of ecosystems in terms of resource and habitat
availability.

423F9A4D8C444066A4B6B29D52CD1B8E.description:
Analyze and interpret quantitative data to construct an explanation for the effects of
greenhouse gases (such as carbon dioxide and methane) on the carbon cycle and
global climate.

C1B53809369B4DA1B069F4486323533A.description:
Develop and use models of the carbon cycle, which include the interactions between
photosynthesis, cellular respiration and other processes that release carbon dioxide, to
evaluate the effects of increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide on natural and
agricultural ecosystems.

443B39DDB244420D947DE347CAE430E1.description:
Conceptual Understanding: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are important
components of the carbon cycle, in which carbon is exchanged between the biosphere,
atmosphere, oceans, and geosphere through chemical, physical, geological, and biological
processes.

9FC976F735E64BC79E256D36F32CCFBA.description:
Use mathematical and computational thinking to support claims that limiting factors
affect the number of individuals that an ecosystem can support.

8E3FE1BA17B04AE3874B8EEC5CBD5D07.description:
Analyze and interpret data that depict changes in the abiotic and biotic components of
an ecosystem over time or space (such as percent change, average change, correlation
and proportionality) and propose hypotheses about possible relationships between the
changes in the abiotic components and the biotic components of the environment.

00F1D2DFBFCA41468E8D13BEE320C506.description:
Conceptual Understanding: Ecosystems have carrying capacities, which are limits to
the numbers of organisms and populations they can support. Limiting factors include the
availability of biotic and abiotic resources and challenges such as predation, competition, and
disease.

651F5636595E441B807816537B4A89EA.description:
The student will demonstrate an understanding that ecosystems are complex,
interactive systems that include both biological communities and physical components of the
environment.

087A78ED25694DE295BBBD469CB677CF.description:

organisms

9EABDF12E27844EF97B7A899A507891C.description:

critically analyze aspects of evolutionary theory.

D79531F07618407990C1061CEC261255.description:

paleontology that underlies the theory of biological evolution

12187E166BA7401A940D046D6BFFCFF2.description: Explain how genetic variability and environmental factors lead to biological evolution.
